summary: SIP sets up sessions between pairs of user agents, so two-party calls are straightforward, but conferences with many participants need more. This document is a framework for how SIP can support conferencing. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4353 describes one way to hold a group conference using SIP. A central focus keeps a separate call relationship with each participant and arranges how their media reaches one another. The document is a framework rather than a complete protocol specification.

questions: how does sip handle conference calls
what is a sip conference focus
what is a loosely coupled conference
subtitle: A focus, conference policy, and media mixers let SIP user agents hold group calls.

tldr.problem: SIP dialogs connect pairs of user agents, so a group conversation needs a way to coordinate many participants and their media.
tldr.mechanism: The framework centers a conference on a focus that keeps a SIP dialog with each participant, applies conference policy, and arranges media through one or more mixers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4353 is an Informational framework describing architecture, terminology, and components. Detailed mechanisms, especially those outside SIP, are left to other specifications.

today: RFC 4353 is an Informational framework published in February 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Three Models of Conferencing
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes loosely coupled, fully distributed, and tightly coupled conferences. A loosely coupled conference can use multicast without a central control point. In a fully distributed conference, each participant has signaling relationships with the others; that model is outside this document.

This framework covers tightly coupled conferences. Each participant connects to one central user agent called the focus, which manages conference functions and may control media mixing.
sections.plainLanguage: Group calls can use multicast, pairwise calls between every participant, or one central focus. This RFC describes the central-focus model.

sections.title: The Focus and Conference Components
sections.content:
The focus is a SIP user agent that maintains a dialog with each participant, forming a star topology. A unique SIP or SIPS conference URI identifies the focus, and requests to that URI are routed to it.

The focus enforces conference policy and uses one or more mixers to provide the media streams. A conference notification service can report changes to subscribers. A logical conference policy server can let clients access policy through a non-SIP mechanism; these roles do not have to be separate physical systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Each participant connects to the focus, which applies the conference rules and arranges the media. The focus can also notify subscribers when conference membership changes.

sections.title: Joining, Leaving, and Changing a Conference
sections.content:
A participant can join by sending an INVITE to the conference URI, subject to the conference policy. Participants leave with BYE; a focus can also add a participant with INVITE or remove one with BYE.

Participants can learn about membership by subscribing to the conference notification service. SIP has no explicit conference-destruction method: a conference can end as a result of its policy, such as when a particular participant leaves. A recording or announcement application can join as another participant.
sections.plainLanguage: A participant joins by inviting the conference URI and leaves by ending the dialog. The conference policy decides who may join and whether a departure ends the conference.

sections.title: Physical Ways to Build the Framework
sections.content:
The logical focus, policy, and mixer functions can be combined or distributed. The RFC describes a centralized server, an endpoint that becomes a focus, a media-server component, distributed mixing, and cascaded mixers.

In distributed mixing, the participants' own mixers can exchange media by unicast or multicast. Cascaded mixers can serve a large conference by connecting each participant to one mixer and linking the mixers under the focus's control.
sections.plainLanguage: The conference roles can live in one server or be divided across endpoints and media servers. The framework allows different physical arrangements while keeping the same logical roles.

sections.title: Authorization and Privacy
sections.content:
Conference policy may limit who can join or who can change policy. Those authorization decisions require authentication; the RFC says normal SIP authentication mechanisms should suffice.

The system may also need to support a participant who listens without being announced or one whose presence is known while their identity is hidden. The framework identifies these as privacy functions the conferencing system needs to provide.
sections.plainLanguage: The focus needs to check who may join or change conference rules. Some conferences also need ways to hide a participant's presence or identity.
